title: More Alzheimer's Research Trouble
body_text: This is a new investigation here at Science that suggests some serious problems in an area of Alzheimer’s work that’s had a lot of attention in recent years. It’s been known for decades that there are mutations in some families and populations that predispose people towards Alzheimer’s-like pathology. I talked about these most recently in this 2023 post, but the subject there was actually on the other side of things: mutations that seemed to be having a protective effect. That’s obviously of great interest. Don’t get me wrong - the mutations that cause extra harm are also very important to learn about, because we need all the clues we can get. But a protective mutation (be it in Alzheimer’s, cardiovascular disease, or whatever) immediately suggests working on its mechanism to see if can be replicated as a therapy in others. It’s intrinsically interesting just as a window into the (still murky) pathology of the disease as well, naturally. This story is about a family in a particular region of Colombia that carries a mutation in the PSEN1 gene, which codes for presenilin-1, a key part of the gamma-secretase enzyme complex that processes the “amyloid precursor protein” (APP) and others. That mutation, E280A, is a terrible thing to carry, because it leads to cognitive decline and full-scale dementia in a persons 40s and 50s. But the reports in 2019 and 2023 report (blogged about above) was about patients that had this mutation along with others that seemed to allow them to partially or completely avoid that fate (!) These mutations implicated pathways involving the reelin and APOE3 proteins, both of which are plausible candidates for involvement in Alzheimer’s pathology. Another report in 2024 showed that only one copy of one of these mutations could be protective as well. The APOE3 one is also known as the Christchurch mutation, since it had shown up in an earlier New Zealand study. This all set off a lot of press coverage, and many readers may well recall seeing some of these articles. It’s set off a lot of research ideas in the Alzheimer’s field as well, up to the point of planning human gene therapy trials and development of potential therapeutic antibody treatments. And such results certainly should get people moving. The idea of a intrinsic protective mutation against Alzheimer’s is extremely compelling, as mentioned above. But the Alzheimer’s research community has been getting worried about how well these reports are holding up. The article references several studies that have looked at other patients carrying these supposedly protective mutations but have gone on to develop Alzheimer’s, and other groups looking for protective mutations have themselves not seen these (reelin and APOE3) showing up as candidates. The concerns really seem to have accelerated in 2023 after Quiroz presented data on Colombian patients carrying one copy of the Christchurch mutation. But some of the cases were people that other neuroscientists had already studied, and the ages of disease onset seemed to have been altered in these new slides. This has called into question the entire procedure used by the Colombian team to evaluate Alzheimer’s symptoms and progression, and unfortunately all of the discrepancies appear to point in the direction of making the patients with the mutated genes look more protected against the disease. These polished-up data points became part of a 2024 paper in the New England Journal of Medicine. One example mentioned is a patient who actual case file mentions being diagnosed with dementia at age 52 when he could no longer put on his own underwear, but the 2023 presentation shows this same person not being diagnosed until age 57. A letter calling these data into question was published in the journal later that same year. That’s been the state of things, and it’s definitely bad enough. But let me quote from the new Science article about what they’ve found now: Science reviewed more than 1000 documents including scholarly papers, patents, grant data, and communications between many of the key researchers, and interviewed more than two dozen independent experts in Alzheimer’s genetics and GNA insiders and collaborators. The investigation suggests the group embraced a dubious approach to identifying protective mutations, improperly changed patient data to tease provocative findings from Christchurch carriers, and published multiple papers containing suspect or copied images. The original authors (Joseph Arboleda-Velasquez of Harvard and Mass Eye and Ear and Yakeel Quiroz of BU and Mass General) have not replied to requests to supply original versions of those now-very-apparently copied images. (The evaluation of the images was done by some of the best in the world at this task - Elisabeth Bik, Kevin Patrick, and neuroscientist Matthew Schrag). Other neurologists contacted by Science agree that there’s definitely something wrong with the images and many say that the problems seem to go well beyond mere carelessness. And this investigative report is turning up employees of the Colombian neuroscience research center who would only speak if their names were withheld because of fear of retribution, which is never, ever a good sign. The authors have been dropping hints about yet another mutation (which they are calling Macondo, after the Colombian town in Gabriel Garcia Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude). Arboleda-Velasquez’s statements in particular are sounding rather grandiose, and the article reports that one of the co-authors of the forthcoming paper (Diego Sepulveda-Falla of Hamburg) on this new mutation has already withdrawn his name from it. He has also gone back to study the work on the previous mutations and has his own doubts. This is obviously bad news on several levels. As the article notes, there are studies in cells and rodent models (not from the authors who are under scrutiny here!) that do show effects of the Christchurch mutation. But taking these all the way up to human effects in Alzheimer's patients, that's a long haul. You have to think that there has been wasted time, effort, and funding chasing after these results based on what looks like a too-hyped-up presentation of them. That's terrible on the face of it, and what's also bad is that the Alzheimer's field really does not need more examples of this sort of thing after the similarly overhyped-with-doctored-images scandal in beta-amyloid research. I find myself explaining to people outside of medicine that no, there really were good reasons to think that amyloid was the cause of Alzheimer's despite all this stuff. But why stop there? Scientific research is under fire in this country (and others), and we don't need more example of misconduct for people to weaponize, either. So what to make of these latest problems scientifically? Even before these revelations, the identification of the reelin and Christchurch mutations as Alzheimer’s “shields” was starting to look too simplistic, for one thing. Human genetics will do that to you. There are indeed single-gene mutations that are the exact cause of some diseases (see the Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease for a canonical list). But so many other disease with a genetic component are far more complicated, with contributions from numerous genes that add up to a disease state when combined with environmental factors. And that goes for protective mutations as well, and even more so. The switch from a functional human gene to a less-functional mutation (as seen in cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s, sickle cell anemia and the other classic genetic-disease examples) are very clear cases. But searching for “better than usual” variants is a much harder task. When you think about it, the way that huge efforts to find such genetic signatures of Alzheimer’s protection have come up short is a very strong signal that the disease does not have such a simple etiology. Unfortunately that means that it is also unlikely to have a simple cure or prophylactic. An awful lot goes on inside a human body after so many decades of life and thousands upon thousands of biochemical systems are affected. Consider the motto of the old herbalists: contra vim mortis non crescit herba in hortis: against death does no herb grow in any garden. There is likely to be no single-shot magic bullet available for the diseases of aging, because we are fighting entropic disorder and breakdown on so many fronts. That doesn’t mean we can’t do better than what evolution gives us - I’m convinced that we can. But when news comes along of some startling breakthrough in preventing such diseases, we all need to remember to look very closely and carefully at what’s being claimed. Wishful thinking is as constant a factor as aging itself.
